questions.question: Classify the costs of Mokoena Backpack Works by traceability and by behaviour, giving examples of each class, and explain which classes enter production cost.
questions.expected_answer: By traceability: direct costs can be followed into the product — canvas, zips and straps are direct materials, the machinists' wages are direct labour, and together they form prime cost. Indirect factory costs that cannot be pinned to one bag are factory overheads: the supervisor's salary, factory rent, electricity, depreciation on sewing machines, insurance, and indirect materials such as oil and needles. Prime cost plus factory overheads gives total cost of production. Administration costs — office salaries, the office telephone — and selling and distribution costs — advertising, delivery fuel, commission — are period costs and never enter production cost. By behaviour: variable costs move with output, like direct materials, direct labour and sales commission; fixed costs ignore output within a range, like rent, the supervisor's salary and depreciation. The two sortings cross: the supervisor's salary is indirect and fixed but still production; commission is variable but never production. The test: factory-for-making is production, office is administration, and reaching customers is selling and distribution.

questions.question: Trace the year's costs through the ledger of Mokoena Backpack Works, from raw materials issued to cost of sales, and calculate the unit cost of production.
questions.expected_answer: Raw materials: opening R72 000 plus purchases R468 000 plus carriage R12 000 gives R552 000 available; less closing R64 000 leaves R488 000 issued — the direct materials cost. Direct labour: wages R342 000 plus employer's contributions R24 000 — R366 000. Prime cost: R854 000. Factory overheads: indirect materials R34 000, supervisor's salary R120 000, rent R84 000, electricity and water R48 000, depreciation R52 000, insurance R18 000 — R356 000. Total manufacturing costs: R1 210 000, taken to work-in-progress. Work-in-progress: opening R38 000 plus R1 210 000 less closing R48 000 gives cost of production of finished goods of R1 200 000. Unit cost: R1 200 000 over 20 000 completed backpacks — R60 per backpack. Finished goods: opening R76 000 plus R1 200 000 less closing R96 000 gives cost of sales of R1 180 000; against sales of R1 770 000 the gross profit is R590 000, exactly 50 percent on cost.

questions.question: Describe the internal controls over materials, labour and overheads in a factory, and explain why ethical costing goes beyond preventing theft.
questions.expected_answer: Materials: buy from approved suppliers at quoted prices; count and inspect deliveries against order and delivery note; lock the store under a named storeman; issue only against signed requisitions; compare what runs should have consumed with what was issued — gaps reveal waste, damage or theft — and control offcuts and scrap, which have value. Labour: clock cards or biometric registers so hours paid are hours worked; overtime approved before it happens; separation between calculating wages and paying them; idle time recorded with reasons. Overheads: budgets per line with monthly comparison, metered readings rather than estimates, and scheduled maintenance. Ethics goes further because a cost saving can conceal harm: cheaper stitching on a bag that carries a child's books is a safety and durability decision, underpaying workers or removing machine guards breaks fair-labour duties, and tipping dye waste into the drain moves costs onto the community — a costing that ignores such shifted costs misstates the true cost of production, and fines or closure eventually return those costs to the business.
